name: Lake George
type: Big, open St. Johns River lake: pilings, jetties, spring runs and returning eelgrass
pool: Set by St. Johns River flow;Mostly under 10 ft, with a deep navigation channel
notes: Coolest water. Bass stage near the spawning flats; specks school offshore.
Spawn starts on warm spells. Big bass move shallow around the moon.
Peak spawn for bass and specks around the full moon.
Post-spawn. Shellcracker spawn on the full moon.
Shad spawn at dawn; bluegill bed on the full moon.
Summer pattern: topwater early, then mats and offshore grass.
Hottest stretch. Fish first light, last light and after storms.
Hottest water. Short bites at dawn and around storms.
Shad move shallow as the nights cool.
Fall feed. Bass school on shad in creeks and canals.
Cold fronts start the speck bite offshore.
Cold fronts. Bass on outside grass; specks school in open water.

flbass.doing: When river flow is high, bass and sunshine bass gather near the jetties at the south end.
how: Live shad or grass shrimp near the rocks.
Texas rig on the drop beside the channel.

fllinesides.doing: Cooler months are best. Stripers and sunshine bass work the south-end jetties, Ninemile Point and the mid-lake pilings, chasing shad.
how: Shrimp-tipped Road Runner or Slab Daddy jig; cut shrimp with a little chum.

specks.doing: Specks school in open water over the deepest flats, channels and offshore grass, suspended at a different depth from day to day.
how: Missouri minnows or grass shrimp, or spider-rig small jigs (hair jigs, tubes, Hal Flies).
Set minnows at several depths, then match the one that bites.
Cast a small jig to schools you see on forward-facing sonar.

bream.doing: Slow. Bluegill and shellcracker hold in deeper grass, canals and around docks; warm, sunny afternoons bring them up.
how: Grass shrimp on the bottom next to hydrilla or eelgrass.
Small jig or worm along canal edges and docks.

flbass.doing: Bass move from the outside grass toward the inside lanes and spawning flats. Warm afternoons pull them shallow; big females stage on the first hard edge.
how: Lipless or flat-sided crankbait ticking hydrilla, vibrating jig or swim jig down grass lanes.
Beaver or jig into pencil reeds and maidencane in 2 to 4 ft.
Wild shiners on the outside edge for big fish.
After a front, fish the closest deeper grass and slow down.

fllinesides.doing: Fish push upriver with the shad on rising spring flows. Current at river mouths, jetties and bends gathers them.
how: Cast up-current with lipless crankbaits and bucktails.
Shad or shiners drifted along the seams.

specks.doing: Schools leave the open water for pad fields, bulrush and Kissimmee grass that sit next to deeper water. A cold front pushes them back out.
how: Troll or drift minnow-tipped jigs along the outside of the pads and reeds.
Minnow under a cork in openings at the grass edge.
Fish the closest open water off the same grass.

bream.doing: Shellcracker move onto firm sand and shell near the grass ahead of the spring full moons; bluegill feed around reeds and docks.
how: Red wigglers on the bottom with a split shot.
Crickets or grass shrimp under a small float along reeds.

flbass.doing: In March, largemouths may still be on beds. Bass gather at the mouths of the west-shore spring runs, and trophy fish move shallow into reeds and bulrush.
how: Short grubs, crawfish and tube baits.
River shiners under a bobber, slow-trolled or free-lined.
Work the mouths at Salt Springs, Silver Glen and Juniper.

fllinesides.doing: Stripers run upriver to spawn; many hold in the current at river mouths and jetties, feeding on shad.
how: Live shad or shrimp on the bottom in the current.
Small spoons and jigs at fish on top.

specks.doing: Specks spawn in pads, bulrush, cattails and Kissimmee grass over sandy bottom, in waves around the full moon, usually at about 60 to 65°F.
how: Minnow or grass shrimp under a small cork in pockets and along reed lines.
A 10 to 14 ft pole and a 1/32 to 1/16 oz jig dipped into holes in the pads.
Fish the closest deeper water off the spawning grass.

bream.doing: Shellcracker bed on the March and April full moons on firm sand and shell near grass. Bluegill start as the water warms.
how: Red wigglers on the bottom; work the area until you find the colony.
Small beetle spin along the edge of the flat.

flbass.doing: Bass move to pilings, jetties, docks and drop-offs in semi-open water. The river shrimp run starts in May.
how: 7 inch worm Texas-rigged on a 1/4 to 3/8 oz sinker, or wacky-rigged in dense pilings.
Live shrimp on a 1/0 hook under a sliding float, cast to the pilings.
Spinnerbait, buzzbait or weedless spoon along the pilings.

fllinesides.doing: As the lake passes the mid 70s, stripers head for cool spring runs and deep holes; sunshine bass school at dawn.
how: Small topwaters and spoons at schooling fish.
Live bait in spring runs and deep holes.

specks.doing: After the spawn, specks scatter to deeper grass edges, docks, bridges and channel edges. The bite slows as the water warms.
how: Minnows at dock pilings, bridges and fish attractors.
Small jig swum along the deep edge of the vegetation.

bream.doing: Bluegill bed in colonies on sand around each full moon from April on: the best bream fishing of the year, with fish near a pound on good lakes.
how: Under a cork over the beds or along reed lines.
In deep spatterdock and grass patches.
Popping bug or small spider at dawn and dusk.

flbass.doing: Pilings and piers hold bass for hours when food and deep water are close. Schoolers work the less-weedy north end around Drayton and Hog islands and the deeper cuts. Live shrimp run May through September.
how: Bass face the current at structure; when it goes slack, move to docks in the backs of coves.
Cast-net 3 to 5 inch shrimp and fish them under a float at pilings.
Chugger or minnow bait at schooling fish.

fllinesides.doing: Warm weather pushes stripers to cool water: spring runs and the Croaker Hole in Little Lake George, a known summer spot.
how: Fish live bait in the cool water.
Stripers and hybrids gather where cool spring water enters.

specks.doing: The slowest season. Specks suspend in the deepest water, on fish attractors and in shade; fish early, late or at night.
how: Lights and minnows at bridges and deep docks.
Vertical jig or minnow at the depth you mark.

bream.doing: Bluegill keep spawning on each full moon; between moons they hold in deeper pads, grass patches and around docks. Fish early.
how: Grass shrimp in deep pads and hydrilla patches; anchor and chum lightly.
Worms and crickets along the walkways.

flbass.doing: Shad and shiners move into creeks, canals and shoreline grass, and bass school on them. Wind-blown grass edges and points fish all day.
how: Lipless crankbait, small walking bait or swimbait at busting fish.
Vibrating jig or spinnerbait on wind-blown grass edges and reed points.
Texas rig or a weightless worm where fish are short-striking.
Shiners on outside edges as the big fish start to feed for the spawn.

fllinesides.doing: Cooling water brings stripers back out; schools chase shad around points, pilings and channel edges.
how: Lipless crankbaits, spoons and bucktails at busting fish.
Live shrimp or shad tight to pilings in current.

specks.doing: Specks pick up later in the fall as the water cools. Willow Cove on the east shore is a standout.
how: Minnows and small jigs across the cove and nearby open water.
Change bait depth until you find the school.

bream.doing: Bream feed hard in the grass as the water cools. Fewer beds, steady numbers.
how: Anchor near a thick hydrilla patch and fish grass shrimp or worms near the bottom.
Crickets under a cork along reed lines.
